title: Carmel, again
tomorrow: at a busy tamale sale, who should get served first?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ignatius found God in the aftertaste of his daydreams: all things. Today, two friends from Carmel who prayed in different ways.

Some friendships run on long voice memos. Others are two people on a couch, saying nothing, completely at ease. Both are real friendship. Prayer has both kinds too, and someone who prays for years may meet both. And inside Carmel, the order of Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross, the two kinds have each had a champion. So: words or silence? Here are the two cases, each in its own voice.
screen: `LONG VOICE MEMOS.` → `OR A QUIET COUCH.` → `WORDS OR SILENCE?`

segments.voice: Teresa speaks first. In her Life, she describes prayer as an intimate sharing between friends: taking time, often, to be alone with the one who you know loves you. She liked to picture Christ beside her, his face, his words, his suffering. And she pushed back on teachers who told people to set aside every image, even of Christ's humanity, in order to rise higher. For her, that was leaving the friend behind. On this view, prayer needs a face and a conversation. John of the Cross answers. In the Ascent of Mount Carmel, he says that a time comes when meditating with thoughts and pictures dries up, and that this can be a good sign. Then the soul should learn to stay with God in loving attention, quietly, without working at images. Forcing words then, he says, only gets in the way. On this view, love grows past words into stillness. The psalm says it in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Be still and see that I am God." Here's the one to tell a friend: Teresa and John weren't rivals. They worked together to renew Carmel, and she called him her little Seneca. They disagree about when to set the pictures down. They agree on the heart of it: prayer is love, paying attention to God.
screen: `TERESA: A FRIEND'S FACE.` · `JOHN: QUIET, LOVING ATTENTION.` · `BE STILL AND SEE.` · `THEY WORKED TOGETHER.` · then, large: `ATTENTION.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and stay still. Let any words or pictures come and go without chasing them, and simply rest your attention on God, or on the quiet itself if that's where you are. When your mind wanders, return gently, the way you'd turn back to a friend on the couch.
Carmel. The order of Teresa and John, named for a mountain, where prayer is loving attention.
Hold onto this: attention, with words like Teresa or without them like John, given in love. Good night.

howItsDone: Carmelite friars and nuns spend set times each day in silent mental prayer; many Catholics learn prayer from Teresa of Ávila's Life and Interior Castle and from John of the Cross.

chat.says: Abuela says real prayer is talking to Jesus like a friend. retreat leader said sit in silence. who's right?
options: Both are Carmelite. Teresa talked with Christ as a friend; John taught quiet attention.
Silence, always. Words are for beginners, so Abuela's way is the lesser one.
Words, always. Sitting in silence isn't really a Catholic way to pray.
chat.meaning: Inside Carmel, Teresa prayed with a friend's face and words, and John taught loving attention in stillness. Both call prayer love paying attention.

Carmel.meaning: a mountain in Israel; the name of the Carmelite order

Teresa of Ávila.meaning: a Spanish nun who renewed Carmel and wrote on prayer

John of the Cross.meaning: a Spanish friar and poet who wrote on dark and quiet prayer

Ascent of Mount Carmel.meaning: John of the Cross's book on the soul's climb to God

Seneca.meaning: an ancient Roman writer, famous for wise sayings
